Cash-cost per egg

=Inputs!$B$2

But where possible, replace estimates with actual receipts — especially feed, because that is usually the biggest recurring cost.

For your first year, use actual egg counts. If you need a forecast while setting it up, enter expected monthly eggs. A rough pattern for six hens might look like this:

To convert a weekly average to a monthly estimate:

=EggsPerWeek*4.345

=(ScenarioCost-ReplacementBaselineCost)/(ScenarioEggs-BaselineEggs)

\]

So the replacement produces extra eggs at roughly 27p each, before allowing for any extra feed, health costs, or egg losses. If your alternative is buying comparable eggs at 30–40p each, replacement may make sense. If shop eggs are 18p each, it probably does not — financially, at least.

• point-of-lay pullets;
• costs of rehoming, dispatching, or keeping retired hens;
• coop/run depreciation;
• egg cartons if selling;

I would keep labour as a separate line rather than mixing it into the main household calculation. Otherwise a pleasant hobby can appear ruinously expensive very quickly.

Also record any offsets separately:

• egg sales;
• sale of hens;
• manure/compost sold or valued;
• value of eggs given to family, if you want to count that as a benefit.

excel
Annual usable eggs: =SUM(I2:I13)
Annual net hen costs: =SUM(M2:M13)
Cost per egg: =AnnualCost/AnnualEggs

Shop equivalent value: =AnnualEggs/12*ShopPricePerDozen

• What your eggs cost to produce
• Whether you would have spent more or less buying similar eggs

Those are not always the same thing, especially if you value better welfare, fresher eggs, particular breeds, or the enjoyment of keeping hens.

prompt: planning out the 200 litre reef build and i want to get the stocking right before i start buying. going by the inch per gallon thing i make it about 20 fish but everyone says thats outdated. i want to work backwards from the skimmer rating and turnover instead. can you set out the maths so i can work out my ceiling and then a list of what to add and in what order
model_response:
You are absolutely right to ditch the "inch per gallon" rule. In marine tanks, that rule falls apart because a 4-inch Tang produces exponentially more waste and requires vastly more swimming space than a 4-inch Blenny.

If you put 20 standard marine fish in a 200-litre (approx. 53 US gallons) tank, it will crash. For a 200L reef, a realistic, healthy stocking level is 6 to 8 well-chosen fish.

Working backwards from filtration and turnover is a much smarter approach. However, because there is no strict algebraic formula (since fish metabolism, feeding rates, and waste vary wildly), we use System Turnover Rates and a Bioload Unit System to calculate your ceiling.

Here is the math, the methodology, and your stocking plan.

Part 1: The Hardware Math & Your Ceiling

First, determine your Net Water Volume (NWV). A 200L display tank minus 20% for rock and sand displacement equals roughly 160L. If you have a 40L sump, your total system volume is back to 200L. We will base the math on 200L.
1. The Skimmer Calculation
Manufacturers notoriously over-rate skimmers. To find a skimmer that dictates your maximum fish ceiling, use the Half-Rating Rule:
• The Math: Look for a skimmer rated for roughly double your system volume for a "light bioload," or specifically rated for your volume at a "heavy bioload."
• Your Target: A skimmer rated for 300L to 400L. If you buy a skimmer rated for 400L, your tank can handle the absolute maximum bioload for its physical size.
2. The Turnover Calculation
For a reef tank, you need two types of turnover:
• Filtration/Sump Turnover: 5x to 10x your volume per hour.
 • Math: 200L x 5 = 1,000 L/H return pump. This dictates how fast waste is delivered to the skimmer.
• Display Flow (Wavemakers): 30x to 50x your volume per hour (depending on coral types).
 • Math: 200L x 30 = 6,000 L/H total internal flow. This keeps detritus suspended so it can reach the skimmer rather than rotting in the sand.
3. Calculating Your Stocking Ceiling (The Bioload Point System)
Since we can't use "inches," let's assign a Bioload Value to fish based on their metabolism, diet (carnivores produce dirtier waste than herbivores), and territory.

Assuming you meet the skimmer and flow targets above, a heavily filtered 200L tank has a Maximum Bioload Capacity of 15 Points.

• 1 Point (Low Impact): Small gobies, firefish, small blennies. (Small, eat little, low waste).
• 2 Points (Medium Impact): Clownfish, Royal Gramma, small wrasses. (Moderate eaters, active).
• 3 Points (High Impact): Dwarf Angelfish, Hawkfish, large wrasses. (Graze constantly, eat a lot, high waste).
• Note: Tangs and large angels are automatic disqualifiers for a 200L due to physical swimming space, regardless of points.

Part 2: The Stocking List (Maxing out at ~14 Points)

Here is a perfectly balanced, colorful, and active list of 7 fish for a 200-litre reef that fits within your 15-point ceiling.

The Lineup:
1. Yellow Watchman Goby (1 Point): Lives in the sand.
2. Royal Gramma (2 Points): Bright purple/yellow, stays near caves/rockwork.
3. Tailspot or Midas Blenny (2 Points): Great personality, perches on rocks, eats algae.
4. McCosker’s Flasher Wrasse (2 Points): Incredibly colorful, active mid-water swimmer (requires a jump lid!).
5. Ocellaris Clownfish (2 Points): Iconic, hosts in an anemone or soft coral.
6. Ocellaris Clownfish (2 Points): Mate for the first one.
7. Coral Beauty OR Flame Angelfish (3 Points): Your centerpiece fish. Beautiful, active, grazes the rocks. (Note: Dwarf angels have a 50/50 chance of nipping at fleshy corals, but are usually fine if well-fed).

Total: 14 Points. You are just under your maximum capacity, giving you a safety buffer.

Part 3: The Order of Introduction

In marine tanks, you must add fish based on territoriality and aggression, starting with the most peaceful and ending with the most aggressive. You should also wait 3-4 weeks between additions to let your biological filtration (beneficial bacteria) multiply to handle the new waste.

Here is your exact timeline:

Phase 1: The Foundation (Peaceful & Bottom Dwellers)
• 1st: Yellow Watchman Goby (Add a Pistol Shrimp with him for a cool symbiotic pairing). He needs time to establish his burrow without being harassed.
• 2nd: Royal Gramma. They need to find a comfortable cave to claim as their own.

Phase 2: The Mid-Water Crew (Semi-Peaceful)
• 3rd: McCosker’s Flasher Wrasse. Very peaceful, but active. Let him get used to the swimming lanes.
• 4th: Tailspot or Midas Blenny. Wait until your tank has been running a few months for this one. They do best when there is a little bit of natural algae growth on the rocks to graze on.

Phase 3: The Bosses (Territorial)
• 5th & 6th: The Clownfish Pair (Add them together). Clowns are damselfish, and once they decide a corner of the tank is theirs, they will defend it fiercely against newcomers.
• 7th: The Dwarf Angelfish (Coral Beauty or Flame). Always add this fish last. Dwarf angels graze constantly and will claim the entire rock structure as their territory. If added first, they will relentlessly bully any new fish added after them.

A final piece of advice before you buy: Build a secure mesh lid. Wrasses, gobies, and blennies are notorious jumpers. A glass lid will trap heat and prevent gas exchange (which lowers pH), so a DIY mesh screen kit is your best friend.

Working Backwards from Bioload Capacity Instead of "Inches Per Gallon"

You're right to ditch that rule — it doesn't account for body mass, waste production, or territorial behaviour. Here's a more defensible way to build your ceiling.
Step 1: Establish Your Real Volume

200L nominal ≠ 200L of water. Subtract:
• Rock/sand displacement: ~15-20%
• Sump volume (if not already counted)

Working water volume ≈ 160-170L (roughly 42-45 US gallons). Use this number for everything below, not the tank's nominal size.
Step 2: Filtration Capacity as the Real Ceiling

Skimmer and turnover don't directly cap fish numbers — they cap dissolved organic load, which is a proxy for total bioload. Here's the logic chain:

Turnover rate:
• Total system turnover (return pump) should hit 5-10x total volume/hour
• On 160L that's 800-1600 L/h through the display
• This handles gas exchange, oxygen delivery, and waste transport to filtration — not stocking directly, but it sets the ceiling for how much waste your system can move

Skimmer rating:
• Manufacturers rate skimmers in tank litres, but their numbers are usually optimistic (marketing for "lightly stocked")
• Realistic rule: pick a skimmer rated for 2x your actual volume for a moderately stocked reef
• On 160-170L, look for a skimmer rated 300-350L

This gives you organic waste removal matched to a moderate bioload — that's your target, not maximum.
Step 3: Convert Filtration Capacity to a Bioload Budget

Since there's no clean formula linking skimmer L-rating to "number of fish," use adult fish mass as the working currency instead of length:

• Estimate each fish's adult size and body mass class (small/medium/large-bodied)
• Small (clowns, gobies, blennies): budget unit = 1
• Medium (dwarf angels, larger wrasses): budget unit = 2-3
• Large/messy eaters (tangs, larger angels): budget unit = 4-5

Total budget for 160-170L with good filtration (skimmer + turnover as above) ≈ 10-14 units

This is a soft ceiling, assuming:
• Weekly 10% water changes
• Good protein skimming as described
• No large messy eaters like tangs unless you go bigger tank later
Step 4: Stocking List — Order of Addition

Add in this order to let biological filtration mature and avoid aggression issues:

| Order | Fish | Adult Size | Bioload Units | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pair of clownfish (captive-bred) | 8cm | 2 | Hardy, first-in, established territory |
| 2 | 2x Firefish or similar goby | 6cm | 1 | Peaceful, low bioload, good early adds |
| 3 | Cleaner shrimp / inverts (CUC) | — | 0 | Not fish, doesn't count against budget but supports system |
| 4 | Royal gramma or similar dottyback | 8cm | 1.5 | Add after territories establish |
| 5 | Coral beauty or similar dwarf angel | 10cm | 2.5 | Add mid-stocking, watch for coral nipping |
| 6 | Flame wrasse or fairy wrasse | 10-12cm | 2.5 | Add later, needs established rockwork to feel secure |
| Running total | | | ~9.5 units | Leaves headroom |

This leaves 1-4 units of headroom for something small later (another goby, blenny, or a small final addition) without pushing past your ceiling.
The Caveats You Need to Hear

• This isn't a precise science — there's no peer-reviewed formula linking skimmer L/h to fish biomass. The "2x skimmer sizing" and "10-14 units" figures are practical heuristics used by experienced reefers, not physics.
• Coral load matters too — if this is a heavily-stocked coral reef, your fish ceiling drops further because corals also draw on the same nutrient export capacity.
• Test, don't just calculate — track nitrate/phosphate after each addition. If they climb before your next scheduled fish goes in, you've hit your real ceiling regardless of what the maths says.
• Behaviour will override maths — the wrasse and angel might just not get along with what's already in there. Livestock compatibility checking still has to happen fish-by-fish.

model_response:
The “inch per gallon” rule is not useful for a reef. A 200 litre tank could be comfortable with 5–8 appropriately sized fish, or overcrowded with three large/active fish. Adult size, swimming space, aggression, feeding load and oxygen demand matter far more than a fish count.

For a 200 L reef, I would plan around a modest mixed-reef bioload, then only increase it if the tank proves it can process the food you are feeding.
1. Start with actual water volume, not the tank’s advertised volume

Use the operating system water volume:

\[
V_\text{net} = \text{display water} + \text{sump operating water} - \text{displacement from rock/sand/equipment}
\]

A “200 L” display often contains only roughly 150–175 L of water once rock and sand are in. If it has a sump, total system volume may end up back around 190–230 L depending on sump size.

Use the actual filled volume when working out dosing, nutrient trends and water changes.

2. Skimmer rating: use it to choose equipment, not to count fish

Skimmer “tank ratings” are not standardised. One maker’s “500 L heavily stocked” skimmer may outperform another maker’s “1,000 L” model.

For a roughly 200 L net system:

• Choose a skimmer rated for roughly 300–500 L on the manufacturer’s heavy-stocked rating, rather than its lightly stocked rating.
• Prioritise a good, consistent model that fits the sump and has a stable water level.
• A skimmer does not set a hard fish limit. It removes some dissolved/particulate organics before they become nitrate/phosphate, but it does not remove all waste and cannot compensate for poor oxygenation, territorial problems or insufficient swimming space.

A slightly oversized skimmer is sensible, but don’t buy a massive unit purely to justify more fish.

3. Turnover: important, but not a stocking calculation

There are two different “turnover” figures.
Return pump / sump turnover

Aim for about:

\[
3\text{–}5 \times \text{display volume per hour}
\]

For a 200 L display:

\[
200 \times 3\text{–}5 = 600\text{–}1,000\ \text{L/h actual flow}
\]

That is actual flow after head height, elbows and plumbing restrictions — not the number printed on the pump box.

More return flow does not mean more stocking capacity. It can make the sump noisy, reduce skimmer contact time and make drains harder to tune.
In-tank circulation

This is provided mainly by wavemakers, not the return pump.

Typical broad starting ranges:

| Reef type | Total in-tank flow |
|---|---:|
| Softies / LPS | 15–30× tank volume/hour |
| Mixed reef | 20–40× |
| SPS-heavy reef | 30–50×+ |

For a 200 L mixed reef:

\[
200 \times 20\text{–}40 = 4,000\text{–}8,000\ \text{L/h}
\]

That should be variable, indirect flow rather than a single jet blasting corals or sand. Again, this supports coral health and gas exchange; it does not directly determine fish capacity.

4. The useful maths: work from food input and measured nutrient trend

Fish produce waste because you feed them. So the practical way to establish your ceiling is:

1. Add livestock slowly.
2. Keep feeding consistent.
3. Measure nitrate and phosphate over time.
4. Stop adding fish when the system cannot hold your chosen nutrient range without excessive maintenance.
Rough feed-to-nitrate calculation

A dry food containing around 50% protein contains roughly:

\[
0.50 \times 0.16 = 0.08
\]

So about 8% of its dry mass is nitrogen.

Nitrogen converted to nitrate equivalent:

\[
1\ \text{mg N} = 4.43\ \text{mg NO}_3
\]

A usable estimate is:

\[
\text{NO}_3\text{ equivalent/day}
=
\text{food g/day}
\times \text{protein fraction}
\times 0.16
\times 4.43
\times \text{waste fraction}
\]

Use a waste fraction of roughly 0.7–0.9 for a conservative estimate.
Example

If you feed 0.4 g dry-food equivalent per day at 50% protein:

\[
0.4 \times 0.50 \times 0.16 \times 4.43 \times 0.8
\]

\[
= 0.113\ \text{g NO}_3
\]

That is roughly:

\[
113\ \text{mg nitrate equivalent/day}
\]

In a 160 L net water volume, with no export at all:

\[
113 \div 160 = 0.71\ \text{mg/L nitrate/day}
\]

In real life, some waste is skimmed, trapped, removed in filter floss, consumed by algae/corals/bacteria, denitrified or exported with water changes. But this shows why “just one more fish” can matter: it is really “more food every day”.
Water-change maths

A water change removes:

\[
\text{Nitrate removed (mg)} = \text{NO}_3\text{ concentration (mg/L)} \times \text{water changed (L)}
\]

Example: 20% weekly change on 160 L is 32 L. At 10 ppm nitrate:

\[
10\ \text{mg/L} \times 32\ \text{L} = 320\ \text{mg NO}_3
\]

That averages about:

\[
320 \div 7 = 46\ \text{mg/day}
\]

So if the system is producing roughly 113 mg nitrate-equivalent per day from food, the remainder has to be handled by skimming, biological export, algae/coral uptake, mechanical removal and other processes. This is why water changes alone are not normally the whole nutrient-export plan on a well-fed reef.

5. Set practical “ceiling” criteria

Do not add fish based on a skimmer rating. Add them until the tank reaches a sensible, stable operating point.

For a normal mixed reef, a reasonable broad target is:

• Ammonia: 0
• Nitrite: 0
• Nitrate: roughly 2–15 ppm, stable rather than climbing
• Phosphate: roughly 0.03–0.10 ppm, stable rather than climbing
• Good pH/oxygen behaviour overnight
• No fish breathing heavily near the surface at night
• No need to overfeed, over-skim, dose carbon, or perform huge water changes just to hold numbers down

After each livestock addition, wait 2–4 weeks while maintaining the intended feeding level. If nitrate/phosphate trend upward week after week despite normal maintenance, you are nearing or beyond the sensible bioload for that setup.

Do not treat “ammonia is zero” as proof that you can add more fish. A mature biofilter will generally process ammonia; the more useful limiting factors are nutrient accumulation, oxygen, swimming space and compatibility.

A sensible 200 L reef stocking plan

Assuming this is a standard 200 L reef with a proper lid, decent rockwork, sump/skimmer and a footprint around 90 cm or more, I would target about six small fish total, with the option of a seventh only if the system performs well.

Here is a deliberately conservative mixed-reef list:

| Fish | Number | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Ocellaris or percula clownfish | 2 | Buy a known pair; captive-bred preferred |
| Yellow watchman goby | 1 | Optional pistol shrimp partner; low open-water demand |
| Royal gramma | 1 | Good cave fish; provide separate rockwork and hiding places |
| Pink-streaked/possum wrasse | 1 | Small, peaceful, needs a lid and a mature tank |
| Tailspot blenny | 1 | Add after the tank has developed natural film algae/biofilm |

That is six fish, but it has a good spread of behaviour and ecological niches: one clown pair, a bottom fish, a cave fish, a small active rock-picker and an algae-grazing blenny.

It will look more natural and usually function better than trying to squeeze in 12–20 small fish.
Suggested order
Before fish
• Fully cycle the tank.
• Run it with lights on long enough to confirm temperature, salinity, pH, flow and equipment stability.
• Have an established quarantine method before buying fish.
• Use a tight-fitting lid; wrasses, gobies and many other reef fish jump.
1. Yellow watchman goby — first fish
Add once the cycle is complete

Just make sure you actually have £500 in the bank for emergencies.

If you are struggling with time (doing those mornings) and money, find a reliable sharer. Someone who pays £25–£35 a week to ride your horse 2 days a week will inject £100+ a month into your budget and give you two days off from yard chores.

Going from 3 to 10 hives is the classic transition from "hobbyist" to "sideliner." It is a massive jump—not just financially, but logistically.

To give you an accurate payback period and figure out the "tipping point" for your time, we need to run the math on the costs, the hidden expenses, and the time commitment.

Here is the breakdown of whether the expansion actually pays.

Part 1: The Financial Math & Payback Period

First, let's look at the costs and revenues for the 7 new hives you are adding.

The CapEx (Upfront Costs per new hive):
• Nuc: 200
• Boxes & Frames: 150
• Total Setup Cost: 350 per hive. (Total for 7 hives = 2,450)

The Gross Revenue (Per hive):
To calculate this, we need to assume a jar size. Assuming standard 500g jars (about 1lb):
• 20kg of honey = 40 jars.
• 40 jars × 12 = 480 gross revenue per hive.

The OpEx (Hidden Ongoing Costs per hive):
Beginners often forget the cost of getting the honey into the jar and keeping the bees alive.
• Jars and lids: ~40 (assuming roughly 1 per jar)
• Custom labels: ~8
• Varroa treatments: ~15
• Winter feed (sugar): ~15
• Total Ongoing Cost: ~78 per hive.

Net Profit per Hive:
480 (Revenue) - 78 (OpEx) = 402 net profit per hive.
The Payback Period:
• The Optimistic Payback: If a new hive produces a full 20kg in its first year, your payback period is 0.87 years (350 setup cost / 402 profit). It pays for itself in the first harvest.
• The Realistic Payback: Nucs usually spend their first season drawing out foundation comb and building up numbers for winter. They rarely produce a 20kg surplus in Year 1. Realistically, Year 1 revenue will be zero (or very low). Therefore, your actual payback period is Year 2.

Part 2: At what point does the time stop being "worth it"?

This is where most sideliner beekeepers get into trouble. You aren't just scaling your honey; you are scaling your labor.

Here is how your time will change, and the exact points where it stops being worth it:
1. The Inspection Tipping Point
• 3 Hives: Takes about 15 minutes to light the smoker and suit up, plus 10 minutes per hive. Total time: 45 minutes a week.
• 10 Hives: Same 15 minutes prep, plus 10 minutes per hive. Total time: 1 hour and 55 minutes a week.
• Is it worth it? Yes. Because your baseline prep time (suiting up, travel to the apiary, getting the smoker going) is now spread across 10 hives instead of 3. Your time-per-hive is actually more efficient at 10 hives than at 3.
• When it stops being worth it: Around 20+ hives. At 20 hives, you can no longer do thorough inspections after work on a weekday before the sun goes down. It consumes your entire weekend.
2. The Extraction Tipping Point (The "Sticky Mess" Factor)
• 3 Hives (60kg): You can extract this in your kitchen in a single afternoon using a cheap 3-frame manual spinner.
• 10 Hives (200kg): 200kg is roughly 15-20 heavy supers of honey. You cannot easily do this in a kitchen. It will take an entire weekend (or two), your house will be covered in propolis and wax, and a manual spinner will wreck your shoulders.
• When it stops being worth it: If you don't buy an electric motorized extractor. If you try to extract 200kg manually, you will hate beekeeping by the end of it. (Note: A motorized extractor costs 400 to 1,000+, which will push your payback period back by another year).
3. The Sales Tipping Point (The biggest hurdle)
• 3 Hives (120 jars): You can sell these to friends, family, and coworkers with zero marketing effort.
• 10 Hives (400 jars): Your friends and family will not buy 400 jars. You now have to actively sell honey. You will need to sit at farmers' markets (spending your weekends), set up a website, or sell to local shops.
• When it stops being worth it: If you are forced to sell wholesale. If you sell to local shops, they will want 40% to 50% margins. Your 12 jar suddenly becomes a 6 or 7 jar. At 7 a jar, your net profit drops to roughly 200 per hive, doubling your payback period and halving your hourly wage.
The Verdict

Financially, going from 3 to 10 hives is a highly profitable move, provided you accept that Year 1 is for building comb and Year 2 is for cash flow. Once established, 10 hives should net you roughly 4,000 a year in profit.

However, it will only remain "worth it" if:
1. You have a plan to sell 400 jars direct-to-consumer at your 12 price point (e.g., a farm gate stall, local Facebook groups, a loyal customer list).
2. You reinvest some of your first year's profits into a motorized extractor and an uncapping tank to save your sanity during harvest.
3. You have space to store 20+ empty supers over the winter without them being ruined by wax moths.

If you have the market to sell 400 jars at retail price, do it. It will pay for itself by the end of the second summer.

Upfront cost for expansion (7 new hives)

• Nucs: 7 × 200 = 1,400
• Boxes/frames: 7 × 150 = 1,050
• Total new capital: ~2,450

(If any of the 3 existing hives need new boxes too, add that in, but I'll assume they're already kitted out.)

Revenue side

20kg per hive, but you sell in jars, not kg — so you need a jar size. Assuming 340g jars (a common size):

• 20kg ÷ 0.34kg ≈ 58 jars per hive
• 58 × £12 = ~£700 revenue per hive, per season

For 7 new hives: 7 × 700 = £4,900/season

That's obviously the gross figure — no deduction yet for jars, lids, labels, sugar syrup feeding, varroa treatment, replacing dead-outs, etc. Realistically knock off £1-2 per jar for packaging/consumables, so more like £550-600 net per hive. Call it £575 × 7 = ~£4,025/season net-ish.

Payback period

2,450 / 4,025 ≈ 0.6 of a season — so technically paid back within the first year, assuming:

• all 7 hives survive and produce a full harvest in year one (unlikely — nucs usually don't give a full crop their first year, more like 5-10kg while they build up comb and stores)
• you actually sell all the jars
• no losses over winter

More realistic first-year scenario

Nucs typically build up rather than produce surplus honeystheir first season. If you get even half a crop (10kg/hive) from the new 7:

• 10kg → ~29 jars → £350 revenue/hive → 7 × 350 = £2,450

That roughly equals your setup cost — so year one is close to break-even, real payback is year two, once all hives are established and hitting full 20kg production.

Where inspections stop being "worth it"

This is really a time-value question, not a money one, since honey sales are decent margin. Think in terms of:

• Time per hive per inspection: call it 15-20 min if you're organized, more if things are going wrong (swarm cells, disease checks, feeding)
• At 3 hives, full inspection round = 45-60 min
• At 10 hives, full inspection round = 2.5-3.5 hours

The question isn't "does honey pay for the time" (it easily does, financially) — it's whether inspecting 10 hives properly in one day/weekend slot is physically feasible for you, especially in swarm season when every hive should ideally be checked within a similar window (7-9 day check cycle). If you're doing this solo around a job, 10 hives means:

• Either longer inspection days, or
• Stretching the cycle to 10-12 days, which increases swarming risk and disease-spread risk

That's where it stops being "worth it" — not because the honey/jar economics turn bad, but because quality of inspection drops past a certain hive count for one person, leading to more swarms lost, more winter losses, more disease — which erodes exactly the yield numbers you're banking on.

Rule of thumb many hobbyist-to-semi-commercial beekeepers use: somewhere around 8-12 hives is the point where you either need a second pair of hands, or you accept some inefficiency (later swarm catches, slightly higher loss rates). Since you're heading to 10, you're right at that edge — doable, but worth having a plan for how you'll compress inspection time (top-bar quick checks, marking queens for faster spotting, staggering apiary sites if hives aren't all in one place).

Bottom line: Financially the payback is fast — under 2 seasons even with conservative first-year yields. The real constraint is your inspection cycle time, not the money. If you can keep every hive checked within 7-9 days through spring, 10 hives works fine. If work/life means that slips to 12+ days per round, you'll likely see it in swarm losses and lower average yield per hive, which is what would actually kill the economics — not the jar price or setup cost.

To judge the move from 3 to 10 hives, focus on the 7 additional colonies.
1. Up-front expansion cost

Per new hive:

• Nuc: 200
• Boxes/frames/setup: 150
• Total: 350 per hive

For 7 more hives:

\[
7 \times 350 = 2,450
\]

So the basic expansion needs about 2,450 up front — before allowing for extractor capacity, extra supers, jars, treatment, feed, losses, transport, etc.

2. Extra honey production

At 20 kg per hive:

\[
7 \times 20 = 140\text{ kg extra honey per season}
\]

Your sales revenue depends entirely on jar size. “12 a jar” needs converting into a price per kg.

| Jar size | Jars per 20 kg hive | Revenue per hive at 12/jar | Revenue from 7 extra hives |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 kg | 20 | 240 | 1,680 |
| 454 g / 1 lb | ~44 | ~528 | ~3,700 |
| 340 g / 12 oz | ~59 | ~706 | ~4,940 |
| 227 g / 8 oz | ~88 | ~1,056 | ~7,392 |

So if you mean 12 for a standard 1 lb / 454 g jar, the additional 7 hives could gross roughly:

\[
140kg \div 0.454kg \times 12 \approx 3,700
\]

per season.

3. Payback period
If jars are 454 g and sell at 12

Gross income per added hive:

\[
20kg \div 0.454 \times 12 \approx 528
\]

Initial cost per added hive is 350, so ignoring annual running costs:

\[
350 \div 528 = 0.66\text{ seasons}
\]

That means the equipment/nuc cost is recovered in well under one good season at that retail price.

But gross revenue is not profit. You need to deduct:

• jars, lids and labels
• sugar/feed
• Varroa treatments
• replacement frames/foundation
• queen replacement/losses
• fuel and delivery/postage
• card fees/market fees
• insurance, extraction and bottling equipment
• the value of your own labour

A more useful calculation is:

\[
\text{Payback seasons} =
\frac{350}{\text{Honey revenue per hive} - \text{annual cash costs per hive}}
\]

For example, at 454 g jars:

| Annual non-labour cost per hive | Approx annual profit contribution per hive | Payback |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 75 | 453 | 0.77 season |
| 125 | 403 | 0.87 season |
| 200 | 328 | 1.07 seasons |
| 300 | 228 | 1.54 seasons |

So, assuming you genuinely sell most of the crop retail at 12 per 454 g jar, the expansion should normally pay back in roughly one season, or one to two seasons if costs/losses are higher or yields are inconsistent.

The important caveat: that is based on a 20 kg crop and selling all of it retail. A poor forage year, queen failure, swarm losses, or difficulty moving the extra 140 kg changes the answer sharply.

4. The sales question matters as much as hive production

Going from 3 to 10 hives means you need to sell an additional:

\[
140kg \approx 308\text{ one-pound jars}
\]

At 12 each, that is about 3,700 of extra annual sales.

Before expanding, ask:

• Can I reliably sell another 300-ish jars at full retail price?
• Will I need wholesale outlets, and at what price?
• How much extra time will bottling, labelling, customer messages, markets and deliveries take?

If you have to wholesale much of it, the economics can change more than the hive-management side. For example, selling at 6–7 per 454 g jar rather than 12 roughly halves the revenue.

5. When do inspections stop being worth the time?

The practical answer is: when the extra profit per hour falls below what you think your time is worth.

Use:

\[
\text{Value of your time} =
\frac{\text{extra annual profit from 7 hives}}{\text{extra hours spent on them}}
\]
A reasonable working example

Suppose each extra hive produces about 528 in sales and costs 125/year in non-labour costs:

\[
528 - 125 = 403
\]

For 7 hives:

\[
7 \times 403 = 2,821
\]

That is the approximate additional annual profit before paying yourself.

Now estimate the added labour. During swarm season, a 10-hive apiary might need perhaps:

• inspections: 10–15 visits × roughly 10–15 minutes per extra hive
• travel/setup/closing-up time
• feeding/treating/queen work
• adding/removing supers
• harvest, extraction, bottling and cleaning
• selling/admin/delivery

The pure inspection component for 7 extra hives might be roughly 15–25 hours per season, depending on apiary layout and inspection style. Once harvest, processing and selling are included, the extra 7 hives may realistically mean 40–80 extra hours per year, sometimes more.

Using the 2,821 figure:

| Extra annual time | Effective return on your time |
|---:|---:|
| 40 hours | ~71/hour |
| 60 hours | ~47/hour |
| 80 hours | ~35/hour |
| 100 hours | ~28/hour |
| 140 hours | ~20/hour |

So if you value your beekeeping time at, say, 25/hour, then the 7 extra hives remain worthwhile provided they take less than roughly:

\[
2,821 \div 25 \approx 113\text{ hours per season}
\]

At 40/hour, your limit is around:

\[
2,821 \div 40 \approx 71\text{ hours}
\]

6. The likely real breakpoint

For most small-scale beekeepers, the extra inspections themselves usually are not what makes 10 hives unprofitable. A well-organised 10-hive apiary is often more time-efficient per colony than 3 hives because travel, smoker lighting, kit preparation and extraction are shared.

The point where it starts not feeling worth it is more often when:

1. You cannot sell the additional honey at retail price;
2. You are constantly firefighting swarms, queen failures or disease;
3. Your extraction/bottling setup is too small, creating a labour bottleneck;
4. The hives are spread across several sites, increasing travel;
5. You price your own labour realistically and find the hourly return too low.

At your stated yield and retail price, 10 hives looks financially sensible if the demand exists. The biggest risk is not the 2,450 setup cost; it is whether you can consistently turn the extra roughly 140 kg / 300+ jars into retail sales.

A simple decision rule:

\[
\text{Expand if }
(\text{retail honey income} - \text{cash costs}) \div \text{extra hours}
>
\text{your target hourly rate}
\]

For a precise result, track this season’s actual hours spent per hive — inspections, extraction, bottling and selling separately — then apply those numbers to the extra 7 colonies.
